planting.note: Pot up offsets after the spring growth flush begins, once roots have dried callus for a day or two.

directions: Grow in a mineral, fast-draining mix under bright filtered light, shielding plants from direct midday sun that can scorch the fine leaf-tip hairs. Water sparingly and let the mix dry fully between soakings, cutting back almost entirely in winter dormancy. The species is named for the short, soft hairs fringing its leaf margins and tips, a texture that is unusual among window-leaved Haworthia and easily felt by running a finger along a leaf edge. It clumps slowly from basal offsets, which can be separated and rooted once they have a few leaves of their own.

planting.note: Repot or divide offsets as new growth resumes in spring, after the dry-season leaf dieback has passed.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil and keep in bright shade; this species gets its name from a striking habit of letting the outer half of its leaves shrivel and die back during the dry season while the inner rosette stays alive, so resist the urge to water it back to green during that rest period. Resume normal watering only once fresh leaf growth appears at the center. It is prized by South African Haworthia collectors specifically for this unusual seasonal dieback adaptation, which mimics drought survival strategies seen in some Lithops.
